title: HRV limits: saturation, confounders and readiness scores
goal: Explain why HRV can mislead (saturation, alcohol, illness, heat), why readiness scores are hard to trust, and how to weigh HRV against how you feel.

steps.title: When higher HRV stops going up
steps.text:
At very high vagal activity, vagal indices of [HRV](g:hrv) stop rising and can fall while resting heart rate gets lower. This is [HRV saturation](g:hrv-saturation). It happens without any sign of fatigue [[c:hl-sat]].

So a falling [rMSSD](g:rmssd) with a falling resting HR can mean more vagal activity, not less [[c:hl-sat-detail]]. Read HRV together with resting HR: a fall in HRV with a falling HR fits saturation; a fall with a rising HR fits lower vagal activity [[c:hl-ratio]].

Saturation mostly matters in very fit athletes with low resting heart rates (the 40s).

claims.text: HRV can fall while resting HR falls, in very fit athletes: saturation.

evidence.quote: the use of specific HRV indices to overcome the issue of HRV saturation in elite athletes (i.e., reductions in HRV despite decreases in resting heart rate)

claims.text: The fall in vagal HRV in saturation goes with low HR and reflects more vagal activity, not less.

evidence.quote: This reduction in vagal-related HRV indices is associated with low HR levels, and is the consequence of an increased, not decreased, vagal activity.

claims.text: In an elite example, a fall in ln rMSSD was read differently depending on how HR changed.

evidence.quote: the decrease during week 7–8 is likely related to a saturation phenomenon (further increase in vagal activity), while that seen at week 9 is more likely related to a decreased vagal activity/increased sympathetic activity

steps.title: A rise can mean trouble too
steps.text:
Many people expect fatigue to lower HRV. The data are less tidy. In a trial of 21 trained male triathletes, all 13 given a 3-week overload block became functionally [overreached](g:overreaching) (test performance fell 9%), and their weekly mean of vagal HRV went up more than in the 8 on normal training [[c:hl-lemeur]].

In the meta-analysis of endurance athletes, resting HRV was largely unaffected by overreaching, and the authors say this may be a methods problem [[c:hl-bellenger]].

So neither direction is a sure sign. An HRV change is a prompt to look at load, sleep, mood and a standard effort, not a diagnosis.

claims.text: In functionally overreached triathletes, weekly means of vagal HRV rose during overload.

evidence.quote: Using daily HRV recordings averaged over each week, this study detected a progressive increase in the parasympathetic modulation of HR in endurance athletes led to F-OR.

claims.text: Across studies, resting HRV was largely unaffected by overreaching.

evidence.quote: Resting HRV is largely unaffected by overreaching, although this may be the result of methodological issues that warrant further investigation.

steps.title: What else moves HRV
steps.text:
HRV is a sensitive but not a specific marker of stress [[c:hl-altini]]. In 28,175 app users (about 9 million morning readings), high alcohol intake went with HRV about 12% lower and heart rate about 6% higher; sickness with HRV about 10% lower and heart rate 6% higher; the menstrual cycle with a 3.2% change in HRV [[c:hl-alcohol-size]].

Even low alcohol doses lowered HRV-based recovery during sleep in 4,098 employees [[c:hl-pietila]]. In heat, vagal HRV can go up after heavy work even as wellness falls [[c:hl-heat]].

Log the usual suspects (alcohol, illness, heat, a late night) next to each reading.

claims.text: HRV is a sensitive but not specific marker of stress.

evidence.quote: Acute stressors analysis revealed how HRV is a more sensitive but not specific marker of stress.

claims.text: High alcohol, sickness and the menstrual cycle each shifted morning HRV by several percent.

evidence.quote: a 6% increase in heart rate (p < 0.05, d = 0.97, effect size = large) and a 12% reduction in HRV (p < 0.05, d = 0.55, effect size = moderate) after high alcohol intake

claims.text: Alcohol lowered HRV-based recovery in a dose-dependent way, even at low doses.

evidence.quote: Alcohol intake was dose-dependently associated with increased sympathetic regulation, decreased parasympathetic regulation, and insufficient recovery.

claims.text: After heavy training in the heat, vagal HRV has risen despite a fall in perceived wellness.

evidence.quote: Under specific circumstances, such as following heavy training loads in the heat, increased, not decreased, vagal-related HRV indices have been observed within 24 h, despite an acute decrease in perceived wellness

steps.title: Readiness scores
steps.text:
Apps and wearables blend HRV, resting heart rate, sleep and sometimes load into one [readiness score](g:readiness-score). Two things to know.

**You can't see inside.** A 2026 review lists growing dependence on proprietary metrics whose algorithms lack transparency among the threats to HRV-guided training [[c:hl-prop]]. You can't tell if a 38 came from sleep, from saturation or from last night's wine.

**It is not the tested thing.** The two guided trials we read used simple rules on HRV alone (a range from the athlete's own readings).

Use a score as one input. Look at the raw HRV, heart rate and your notes behind it.

claims.text: Proprietary readiness metrics with opaque algorithms are a threat to sound HRV-guided training.

evidence.quote: growing dependence on proprietary metrics whose underlying algorithms lack transparency and may oversimplify training decisions

steps.title: HRV against how you feel
steps.text:
Do HRV and your own feelings agree? Often not. In a review of 56 studies, subjective and objective well-being measures generally did not correlate, and self-reports tracked training load with more sensitivity and consistency [[c:hl-saw]].

In 39 adults tracked for 3 months, self-reported stress and nervousness had no link to overnight HRV; feeling 'energised' went with lower HRV [[c:hl-ungaro]]. That study was funded by a drinks maker and was observational, so treat it as weak.

So don't override a clear wellness answer with a number, and don't ignore HRV. When they disagree, go to a third source: a standard session. This is advice, not a trial result.

claims.text: Subjective and objective well-being measures generally did not agree; subjective ones tracked training load more sensitively.

evidence.quote: Subjective and objective measures of athlete well-being generally did not correlate. Subjective measures reflected acute and chronic training loads with superior sensitivity and consistency than objective measures.

claims.text: Daily self-reported stress and nervousness were not associated with overnight wearable HRV.

evidence.quote: Self-reported stress and nervousness did not have an association with heart rate variability

points: At very high vagal activity HRV can fall while resting HR falls (saturation): read HRV with resting HR and your own history.
A rise in vagal HRV can come with overreaching; resting HRV was largely unaffected in the pooled data. Neither direction is a sure sign.
Alcohol (about −12% HRV after a lot), sickness (about −10%), the menstrual cycle and heat all move HRV: log them beside each reading.
Readiness scores hide their formula and blend signals; treat them as one input, not a verdict.
HRV and how you feel often disagree; use a standard session as the tie-breaker.

options.text: At very high vagal activity, HRV indices stop rising and can fall as resting HR gets lower
options.why: Right: a fall in HRV can then mean more vagal activity, not less.

options.text: The sensor memory fills up and stops recording beats
options.why: Saturation is a physiological effect, not a device fault.

options.text: Fatigue makes HRV rise instead of fall
options.why: That describes a different finding, the rise seen in overreaching.

options.text: Sympathetic overactivity pushes HRV down in tired athletes
options.why: Saturation happens without sympathetic overactivity or fatigue.

variants.stem: Over 12 weeks of base training a cyclist's resting heart rate falls from 52 to 46 beats·min⁻¹ and his morning rMSSD slips from 85 to 78 ms. He feels fresh and his power is rising. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Overreaching: the lower HRV shows sympathetic overload in his body
options.why: A falling HR and good form argue against overload.

options.text: Possibly saturation: more vagal activity, so the HRV dip is no fatigue sign
options.why: Right: reductions in HRV with falling resting HR can reflect more vagal activity.

options.text: Sensor error, since a fitter heart must always show a higher HRV
options.why: HRV can fall at very high vagal activity; that is saturation, not a sensor fault.

options.text: Detraining: a lower rMSSD means his heart has become weaker
options.why: His power is rising, which points away from detraining.

variants.stem: A runner's resting HR falls from 48 to 44 beats·min⁻¹ over a block, her rMSSD slips from 90 to 82 ms, and her pace at a given effort improves. How should she read the rMSSD dip?

options.text: As proof that she has become non-functionally overreached
options.why: Improving pace and a falling HR do not fit it.

options.text: As a recording artefact that she should ignore every time
options.why: Check for artefacts, but the pattern fits a known effect.

options.text: As possible saturation, checked against her HR and how she feels
options.why: Right: with a falling HR and improving pace, the dip fits saturation.

options.text: As a sign her vagal activity has dropped
options.why: In saturation, vagal activity is higher, not lower.

variants.stem: In a 3-week overload block, a triathlete's weekly mean ln rMSSD rises while her run-test performance falls 9%. Which statement fits the evidence best?

options.text: A rise always means she is fresh, so the test result must be wrong
options.why: The trial shows rises alongside lost performance.

options.text: Overload always lowers HRV, so the data are an error
options.why: Pooled data found HRV largely unaffected, and this trial found a rise.

options.text: Weekly means are useless, only single days count
options.why: Isolated readings missed what weekly means caught.

options.text: A rise in vagal HRV can accompany functional overreaching, so a rise alone does not show good recovery
options.why: Right: in the trial, weekly means of vagal HRV rose in overreached triathletes.

variants.stem: A cyclist's HRV rises during a heavy training camp while his sprint power falls. What is the sound conclusion?

options.text: Don't read the rise as recovery: check load, sleep, mood and a standard effort
options.why: Right: HRV can rise with overreaching, and resting HRV may not change at all.

options.text: The rise proves he is adapting, so add more load
options.why: A rise is not proof of adaptation.

options.text: The power drop is noise, since HRV is the objective measure
options.why: A performance fall is a key signal.

options.text: HRV cannot change with training
options.why: It can; the question is how to read it.

variants.stem: A cyclist's 7-day mean rMSSD is 64 ms. The morning after a night of heavy drinking it is 56 ms. What is the percent change?

options.why: Right: (56 − 64) ÷ 64 = −0.125, about the size of the drop reported after high alcohol intake.
This divides by today's 56 instead of the baseline 64.
This reads the 8 ms drop as a percent.
This drops the sign: rMSSD fell, it did not rise.

variants.stem: A runner's baseline rMSSD is 75 ms and the morning after a few drinks it is 66 ms. What is the percent change?

options.why: This divides by today's 66 instead of the baseline 75.
This reads the 9 ms drop as a percent.
This drops the sign.

variants.stem: A triathlete's baseline rMSSD is 90 ms and she records 81 ms with a cold coming on. What is the percent change?

options.why: This divides by today's 81 instead of the baseline 90.
This reads the 9 ms drop as a percent.
This drops the sign.

variants.stem: The morning after a big night out, a runner's rMSSD is 12% below baseline. Normal day-to-day variation is also about 12%. What does this tell you?

options.text: Alcohol caused the entire drop and nothing else could have done
options.why: A drop of this size also occurs with no cause at all.

options.text: The drop is too small to matter, so alcohol has no effect on HRV
options.why: Large studies show alcohol lowers HRV; it just is not visible in one day.

options.text: HRV is useless for any athlete who ever has a drink
options.why: Averaged and logged, it still carries signal.

options.text: It is about the size of normal noise: log the alcohol and watch the trend
options.why: Right: effects of this size sit inside ordinary scatter, which is why context and averaging matter.

variants.stem: In 4,098 free-living Finnish employees, what did alcohol do to HRV-based recovery during the first hours of sleep?

options.text: It lowered it in a dose-dependent way, even at low doses
options.why: Right: the effect grew with the dose and showed up at low intake too.

options.text: It lowered it only after heavy drinking
options.why: Effects were seen with low intake as well.

options.text: It raised it, because alcohol relaxes you
options.why: Alcohol was linked to less parasympathetic and more sympathetic regulation.

options.text: It had no effect in physically active people
options.why: Regular activity did not protect against the effect.

variants.stem: A triathlete finishes a hard session in 32 °C heat. Next morning her rMSSD is above her average, yet she reports heavy legs and a low mood. How should she read this?

options.text: Her HRV is the objective answer, so she has fully recovered
options.why: Wellness fell although HRV rose, so the two disagree.

options.text: HRV can rise after heavy heat work while wellness falls, so it is no proof of recovery
options.why: Right: HRV and how you feel can point in opposite directions after hard training in the heat.

options.text: Her HRV is wrong, because heat always lowers HRV in everybody
options.why: Vagal HRV has risen after heavy training in the heat.

options.text: Her feelings are wrong and should be ignored
options.why: A drop in perceived wellness is a real signal too.

variants.stem: A cyclist in a hot training camp sees his morning HRV climb for three days while he feels flat and sleeps badly. What is the best response?

options.text: Raise the load, since HRV shows he is recovering fast
options.why: A rising HRV is not proof of recovery here.

options.text: Stop using HRV for the rest of the camp
options.why: It is still useful if read with other measures.

options.text: Don't take the rise as recovery; weigh how he feels and run a standard effort
options.why: Right: after heavy loads in the heat, HRV can rise despite a drop in perceived wellness.

options.text: Ignore the way he feels because HRV is rising
options.why: Wellness answers matter and often track load better.

variants.stem: On the morning of a key race, a runner's ring gives a readiness score of 38 out of 100. How should she use it?

options.text: Cancel the race, because the score is a validated fatigue test
options.why: The formula is not published and was not what the trials tested.

options.text: As one input beside her heart rate, how she feels and recent training, since the formula is hidden
options.why: Right: with an opaque formula you can't tell what drove the 38.

options.text: Ignore it, because HRV never relates to fatigue
options.why: HRV can carry information; the issue is the opaque blend.

options.text: Trust it over how her legs feel, since it is objective
options.why: Feelings and HRV often disagree, and neither is automatically right.

variants.stem: Two apps give the same cyclist readiness scores of 82 and 55 on the same morning. What best explains the gap?

options.text: Each app blends inputs with its own hidden formula, so neither is a ground truth
options.why: Right: undisclosed algorithms and weightings can give different scores from the same data.

options.text: One app is measuring his heart and the other is not
options.why: Both use similar inputs; the difference lies in how they blend them.

options.text: The higher score must be right because it is better news
options.why: Neither can be checked without the formula.

options.text: Readiness changes by 27 points between two breaths
options.why: The day-to-day change is not the issue; the formulas differ.

variants.stem: A cyclist's HRV and 7-day mean are normal, but he wakes flat with heavy legs, and intervals are planned. What is the best plan?

options.text: Take the feeling seriously: shorten or ease the session, or test with a warm-up before deciding
options.why: Right: normal HRV does not rule out fatigue, and self-reports track load well.

options.text: Do the full intervals: objective data beat feelings
options.why: Subjective measures were at least as sensitive to load as objective ones.

options.text: Stop training for a week because normal HRV hides an illness
options.why: One flat morning does not justify a week off.

options.text: Re-measure until HRV matches how he feels
options.why: Repeating the test until it fits is not a method.

variants.stem: A runner feels great, but this morning her rMSSD is 15% below her 7-day mean after a night of heavy drinking and a late flight. Intervals are planned. What is the best plan?

options.text: Cancel the intervals: HRV is below range, so it must be fatigue
options.why: Alcohol and travel can lower HRV without real fatigue.

options.text: Ignore HRV forever, since it moved without a training cause
options.why: It still carries information; it just needs context.

options.text: Log the likely causes and use a warm-up check: if it feels easy, go ahead
options.why: Right: HRV can be moved by alcohol and travel; the feeling and a standard check decide.

options.text: Add extra volume to use the good feeling
options.why: A good feeling is not a reason to add load on a poorly understood signal.

variants.stem: Ungaro 2026 followed 39 healthy adults for 3 months and found no link between self-reported stress and overnight wearable HRV. It was funded by a sports-drink company. Which limit most affects how far to trust it?

options.text: It used a wearable, so no wearable-based result is ever valid
options.why: Wearables can produce usable data; accuracy varies by device.

options.text: It lasted 3 months, which is too long to give useful data
options.why: Longer follow-up is a strength.

options.text: It used self-reports, which are always completely accurate
options.why: Self-reports have their own errors, so agreement is not guaranteed.

options.text: It is observational, small (39) and funder-linked, so it can't say which is right
options.why: Right: the funder, size and design all limit what it can say.
